title: Car stocks: how to analyze automakers in the transition
description: Car stocks: P/E 6 at Volvo Cars, 334 at Tesla, nonexistent at Polestar. How to analyze automakers — cycle, gross margin, cash and multiples.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Car stocks are shares in companies that develop, build and sell passenger cars — the stock market's veteran cycle industry and clearest disruption field at once. World production reached 96.4 million motor vehicles in 2025, up 3.9 percent, says industry organization OICA — and one in four newly sold cars was electric, says the IEA's Global EV Outlook. AK1A's universe has four anchors: Volvo Cars among volume makers, Tesla and Polestar on the electric side, fuel cell supplier PowerCell. Their valuations span P/E 6 to nonexistent — same industry, three pricing worlds. As always here: education in method, never advice about individual stocks.

## What are car stocks — an industry with two clocks

A passenger car is the household’s second-largest purchase after the home — and postponable. When rates rise or job security falls, new-car sales decline: the first clock, a classic business cycle. The second runs slower but deeper: combustion to electric, changing cost structure, competition and value chain at the root. Car analysis holds both clocks — the cycle explains this year's swings, the transition who has a business model in ten years.

A delimitation: trucks and buses (Volvo Group, Scania) belong to industrial analysis — here it is passenger cars and their suppliers.

The business model in one line: capital-intensive volume manufacturing with a thin gross margin. The universe's two profit-making automakers show it: Volvo Cars gross margin 15.6 percent, Tesla's 18.9 percent (raw data September 2026). The universe's highest, LVMH's 66 percent, sits more than three times higher. Thin margins on large volumes is the industry's construction — and why its ratios are read in a different order than for software: volume, margin, cash — valuation last.

## Car stocks in three valuation worlds — from P/E 6 to nonexistent

The four anchors are priced in three different worlds:

**Volvo Cars: P/E 6.0 and P/B 0.37.** The price pays six years of current earnings — yet EV/EBIT sits above 21. How? The 2025 operating result nearly disappeared: EBIT margin 0.8 percent, and a multiple with an almost zeroed denominator misleads both ways — [the P/E ratio's known trap](/kurser/km-009-pe): at a cycle bottom E is lowest exactly when the price looks cheapest, while [EV/EBIT](/kurser/km-010-evebit) shows a different picture.

**Tesla: P/E 334 and PEG 4.3.** The reverse: the price pays not for today's cars but for a story about energy storage, software and self-driving — revenue not yet in the income statement. With [PEG 4.3](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026) the price pays heavily for that story; the multiple asks what must happen.

**Polestar: P/E lacks a denominator.** With a negative result there is no profit to divide by. Analysis moves to [the P/S ratio](/blogg/ps-tal-nar-ar-det-anvandbart) and, above all, to cash: how long does the money last? A question of financing, not valuation.

The lesson: never compare multiples without asking what the denominator is worth — P/E 6 with collapsing E and P/E 334 with story-based E are both question marks.

## The cycle mechanics — margin leverage worked through

The core risk is fixed costs: factories, platforms, development — they make the result a servant of volume and price. A worked example with invented but realistic numbers:

A factory builds 300,000 cars a year at an average price of 400,000 kronor. Variable cost per car: 340,000 kronor. Fixed costs: 12 billion kronor a year.

- Revenue: 300,000 × 400,000 = 120 billion kronor.
- Contribution margin: 300,000 × 60,000 = 18 billion.
- Operating income: 18 − 12 = 6 billion — an EBIT margin of 5 percent.

Two stress cases. Volume falls 15 percent (255,000 cars): contribution drops to 15.3 billion, the result to 3.3 billion — 45 percent less result on 15 percent less volume; leverage three times. Instead let prices fall 5 percent (380,000 kronor per car, unchanged volume): contribution drops to 12 billion, the result to zero — a 5 percent price fall erases the whole operating income.

The mechanics show in the universe series: Volvo Cars fell from 15.4 billion kronor result in 2024 to essentially zero in 2025; Tesla's profit roughly halved two years running — 15.0 billion dollars 2023 to 7.1 and 3.8, that is −53 and −46 percent. Same factories; only volume and price moved. Margin swings are deepened in [EBITDA margin analysis](/blogg/v08-ebitda-marginal-analys).

## The electric transition — a line-item question, not a story

The IEA put 2025 global electric sales at more than 21 million cars — above 20 percent growth in a year, one in four new cars — and projects around 23 million for 2026. China built 34.5 million of the world's 96.4 million vehicles in 2025, where the electric share is highest. The transition is reality — it shows up in the accounts, line by line: gross margin direction (battery cost against price pressure), the electric share of deliveries, development cost as a share of revenue. Tesla's price cuts are the textbook example: when demand softens and supply grows, price becomes the volume lever — [the gross margin](/blogg/v07-bruttomarginal-analys) is the thermometer showing it before the annual result.

The transition also lowers the moats: an electric driveline has a fraction of a combustion engine's parts, and new entrants — especially Chinese — take share at a pace the industry has not seen. Historical margins are a weaker guide here than in many industries: not only "where is the margin today" but "why would it persist" — the moat logic of [revenue stability analysis](/blogg/v12-intaktsstabilitet-analys).

## The cash clock — the loss-makers' second clock

For companies not yet profitable, the analysis moves to cash. Polestar reported a 2025 loss of 2.4 billion dollars — roughly 200 million a month — and universe data measures the cash runway at around 15 months. You calculate it: current cash divided by monthly burn. A runway under a year or two makes financing — share issue, loans or a partner — the main driver before the product question; every new issue dilutes existing owners. The mechanics are covered in [the emission risk course](/kurser/rk-02-emissionrisk) and [capital burn analysis](/blogg/v19-kapitalforbranning-analys).

The fourth anchor shows the value chain's third position: PowerCell builds no cars but fuel cells for industry — a different model: gross margin 30.6 percent (double the automakers'), positive cash flow, revenue grown from 245 to 385 million kronor over four years, the loss shrinking. The supplier position shifts the risk from volume cycle to technology and customer risk — "the car sector" is several games depending on where in the chain the company stands.

## Reading the reports for car stocks — five points

- **Delivery volumes first.** Automakers report production and delivery numbers every quarter — the industry's fastest pulse. Compare with the same quarter last year and expectations.
- **Gross margin direction.** A margin squeezed while volumes hold is price pressure; a margin holding while volumes fall is cost discipline — different implications.
- **Geographic mix.** Margins and volumes per region show where the cycle strikes — and exposure to tariffs and currencies.
- **Free cash flow and capital spending.** Factories and platforms are the industry's investments; watch if capital spending grows faster than revenue.
- **For loss-makers: cash runway and the issue trail.** Monthly burn, the cash pile and the issue history say more than any multiple.

The full reading order is in [the quarterly report course](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten); [our Volvo Cars walkthrough](/blogg/hur-vi-analyserade-volvo-cars) shows a complete analysis in practice.

## The summary

- Car stocks run on two clocks: the business cycle (this year's result) and the electric transition (the decade's business model).
- Margin leverage is the core risk: volume −15 percent meant result −45 percent, and a price fall of 5 percent erased the result entirely.
- Same industry, three pricing worlds: P/E 6 with a collapsed result, P/E 334 with a story-carried result, and P/S-cash analysis where the result is missing.
- For loss-makers the cash runway (Polestar: around 15 months) is the first number — multiples the second.
- The value chain separates the games: manufacturer, newcomer and supplier have different risk pictures.

To go further: [the car sector course](/kurser/se-09-bil) covers disruption and the electric shift in depth; [the complete guide](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026) sets the method in context.
